title: Show HN: Rhun, an open-source code editor written in assembly
text:
I found that I'm not using even 1/3 of vim/vscode features anymore.

That's wht I'm building rhun - a small code editor for Linux, Windows and Apple silicon Macs. It obviously has Vim mode, a terminal, Git diffs and a panel for Claude Code or Codex sessions.

The editor and pixel renderer share an x86-64 assembly core. For Apple silicon, a build-time translator converts that core to AArch64, with separate platform adapters around it. The latest release can draft commit messages using a local Ollama model or an existing Claude Code or Codex subscription.

It's a solo project, MIT licensed and still early.

title: Re: Etymon – Get rid of all your Claude.md, AGENTS.md,...
text:
I use a bunch of different harnesses depending on model need, usage limits, harness-specific capabilities, and other factors. I often switch between ClaudeCode for heavy coding, hit the 5hr limit, switch to Codex to finish it up. If I'm at limits for all, I'll go to OpenCode(DeepSeek) and finish up there.

This is a great problem to have, coding has never been easier. But, it also introduces a problem that I've had issues with for a while. The whole ecosystem is fragmented.

- CLAUDE.md - .github/copilot-instructions.md - AGENTS.md - .opencode/opencode.json - .mcp.json - .codex/config.toml - .github/mcp-config.json - .cursor/rules/ - .claude/rules/ - .agents/skills/ - .github/skills/

And this is just picking on a few of the popular harnesses. Bring in Antigravity, Roo, Cline, Zed, Gemini, Pi, Amp, you name it, and it just gets even more fragmented. Now, we're maintaining 20+ files just to make a project portable for other developers using their preferred harness.

We're doing better at converging onto standards (e.g. SKILSL.md, Agent Plugin Spec, MCP spec, AGENTS.md) but there's still overall fragmentation in where these files exist, what clients support the standard, what interfaces the standards support (e.g. Agent Plugin Spec only supports skills/MCP, not hooks or agents). Overall, it's messy.

So, I built Etymon. It's goal is very simple. Convert via `etymon convert` all your existing harness-specific files into a single, understandable unit (`etymon.toml`). Then, anyone can sync it to their harness via `etymon sync --harness codex`, for example. No need to track all these different files, just track `etymon.toml` and `etymon.lock` and profit.

And the goal here is not a new standardization. Etymon uses existing standards where possible (like SKILLS.md and MCP registry), so it's simply a wrapper around these standards. As new standards become the norm (such as Agent Plugin Spec), Etymon will adopt those. The eventual goal is Etymon won't be needed anymore: all interfaces (Skills, Agents, MCP, Hooks, Plugins) have standard specs at standard locations, and all major clients have adopted the standards. Until then, Etymon serves as a bridge for that gap.

Looking for some validation with Etymom though. Surely it isn't just a problem I face, so hoping to get it in front of others and test it in the real world. Any feedback (even if it's "This sucks!!!!"), comments, questions, or whatever is greatly appreciated!

title: Re: Apex, a coding model specialized in mobile and web...
text:
Hi HN, I’m Michal. Together with Piotr, Artur, Lech, and Mike, for the last 8 months we've been building Apex, a coding model for mobile and web development. A model which we trained on React Native expertise and turned out to be good at React web too.

We're a small R&D team at Callstack, where we spend a lot of time working on React Native apps and create open-source libraries. We wanted to see how far that experience could take an open-weight model through domain-specific training. Could we achieve frontier-level performance for specific tasks at a much lower cost? After a few base model iterations, we sticked to Qwen as a foundation, trained on curated framework documentation, source code, APIs, and repository-grounded conversations, evaluated by our engineers.

On our React Native Evals (rn-evals.vercel.app), Apex scores 87.8%, compared with 88.6% for Claude Opus 5.5. The reported evaluation cost is $7.72 versus $28.75. These are our benchmarks, so we’d encourage you to try tasks from your own repository too.

Over the weekend we released a stealth version of Apex, Pixel Canary on Vercel AI Gateway. In Vercel’s Next.js evaluation, that preview passed 28 of 31 tasks, or 30 with documentation in context, matching GPT-6 Astra. Opening free access to the model on AI Gateway smashed our infrastructure and in these first days Pixel Canary was slow. We're not DevOps by train, but over these 5 days we had a quick crash course on scaling the model performance on B200s with custom prefill and decode setups to optimize load accordingly to the traffic we made, allowing us to achieve ~100 TPS at 4s p50 latency on the last day, with up to 80B tokens / day throughput.

The API is now available for business users (we need few more weeks to sort out EU consumer rights). It works with OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible coding tools. We charge $0.50/M input, $0.20/M cache, and $3/M for output.

We’re interested in where specialization pays off and where it falls short. We're planning more specialized models for native iOS and Android development, and more.

I'm using this model for other languages and it's just as good as running Sonnet or Sol on medium. It's still Qwen, but tuning seems to make it better than barebones version on coding tasks.

If you try it, I’d love to hear which tasks it handles well and where you still reach for another model.

title: Re: Figma restricts MCP access to whitelisted clients,...
text:
For context: Figma has two MCPs. The local "dev" MCP that works through the Desktop app, and the remote MCP that requires a connection to Figma. Companies need to be whitelisted to use the remote MCP, which is the only one that allows agents edit access to Figma documents.

I only found out about Figma's limitation when I was trying to add the remote MCP server to GitHub Copilot Desktop and kept running into errors. Turns out they whitelisted GitHub Copilot CLI but not the Desktop app and had put a pause on enabling any more vendors. Eventually someone (not sure which side) got it working.

Kind of strange to limit edit access only to the Remote MCP when their competitors like Pen[1] and Paper[2] allow any local agent to edit.

[1] https://www.pen.dev/

[2] https://paper.design/

title: Re: Ask HN: Who wants to be hired? (October 2026)...
text:
Location: Prague, Czech Republic (CET)
  Remote: Yes; hybrid works too
  Willing to relocate: Open to discuss
  Technologies: Go, TypeScript/React, Electron, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes (RKE2), GCP, Linux, MCP / agentic tooling
  Résumé/CV: on request by email
  Email: editor678@gmail.com
My rollback time is measured in kilometres.

I build self-service kiosks and the POS systems next to them. Real machines, bolted to a shop floor, kicked by customers, unplugged by the cleaner, on whatever internet the landlord is paying for. When a release goes wrong there, nobody types git revert. Somebody gets in a car.

So most of my work is the unglamorous half. Provisioning that takes a device from cardboard box to live fleet with nobody touching a keyboard. OTA updates that can lose power mid-flash and still boot. One codebase that satisfies several certifiers, because the alternative is a fork per market and death by cherry-pick.

The day job for the last few years: ~12 engineers across backend, frontend and QA, most of them hired by me, all of their PRs still read by me. I also built the team's Claude Code setup — CLAUDE.md hierarchies, MCP servers for Jira/GitHub and codebase search, fan-out review with parallel subagents — and got twelve people to actually use it, which was the harder engineering problem.

Looking for: engineering manager, tech lead, or staff-level backend. Remote, EU hours. I'm at my best where software meets physical objects, auditors, or a team that ships but can't tell you when.

Languages: English, Czech. Contractor (B2B) or employee.
